title: Zoning data APIs for U.S. parcels and site selection
description: Compare Zoneomics, Gridics, Regrid and city GIS APIs. Use a Staten Island tax lot with five mapped zoning districts to test a vendor’s parcel lookup.
coverAlt: Aerial map of 2239 Forest Avenue in Staten Island. Five colored areas show the share of the tax lot in each base zoning district. The published point falls in C8-1.
coverCaption: 2239 Forest Avenue, Staten Island. The white line traces the MapPLUTO tax lot. Colors show the clipped NYC zoning polygons. Aerial imagery from USDA, USGS and The National Map.
intro: For a U.S. parcel zoning lookup, compare Zoneomics for point and area queries, Gridics for development standards in supported jurisdictions, and Regrid for zoning fields attached to parcel records. Keep the local government’s map and ordinance as your reference. At one Staten Island address, a point lookup gives one district, the city’s tax lot record lists three, and a boundary overlay finds five.
takeaways: Decide whether you need zoning at a coordinate, a parcel summary, or each district intersecting the site.
Ask how the API handles small overlaps and where its source shows the adopted map and rule.
Verify the zoning lot, applicable rules and approvals with the local authority before committing to a use or floor area.

sections.heading: Which zoning API fits the work?

blocks.text: Give every provider the same parcel boundary and proposed use. The commercial comparison below uses published documentation. The five-district result comes from the city data queried for this article.

columns: What to check in a trial
rows: Zoneomics
Point and area lookups, with published options for use tables, controls and overlay data where available.
Submit the parcel polygon and ask for the geometry, source date and permitted-use reference for the affected portion.
Gridics
Parcel-level zoning, uses, setbacks and modeled development capacity.
Check jurisdiction coverage and ask which source rules and parcel assumptions drive a building envelope or floor-area result.
Regrid
Parcel IDs with local zoning codes, standardized categories on applicable plans and a matched zoning product.
Ask when you receive one parcel code, how the code is assigned and which product supplies more detail or a link to the city code.
Invariant Earth
A coordinate lookup returns parcel identity and a Regrid-sourced zoning code alongside other location fields.
Review the matched assessor parcel number. The published catalog allows a nearest-parcel fallback for parcel matching. Use the city district geometry to test the whole tract.
Municipal GIS and code
Local tax maps, district polygons, overlays and the adopted map and ordinance. Format and update process depend on the jurisdiction.
Confirm map and ordinance dates independently. Ask the authority which zoning lot and approvals apply to your plan.

sections.heading: One Staten Island parcel, three different lookup results

blocks.text: We used the MapPLUTO 26v2 boundary for 2239 Forest Avenue, Staten Island, borough-block-lot 5012500011. We also queried NYC Planning’s base zoning district polygons on November 23, 2026. The published parcel point falls in C8-1. MapPLUTO lists M1-1, C4-1 and C8-1 in that order and flags the parcel as split.

The polygon overlay finds five intersections. C4-1 and M1-1 each cover a little over 37% of the mapped tax lot. R3A and R3-2 together cover 7.17%. Both individual shares fall below the 10% minimum defined for MapPLUTO’s base district fields. The two largest districts switch order between the parcel fields and this overlay. The largest areas differ by only 0.35 percentage points in our calculation. Keep the original parcel fields and recomputed results with their own source dates.

blocks.text: We projected the boundary and zoning polygons to New York State Plane Long Island in U.S. survey feet, intersected each district with the tax lot and divided by the mapped polygon area. The total is approximately 378,715 square feet. MapPLUTO’s separate LotArea field is 376,110 square feet. Use the polygon area as the denominator when reproducing these shares. Displayed percentages may differ from 100% because of rounding.

sections.heading: What should a zoning API return before you rely on it?

columns: What a usable result gives you
rows: Parcel identity
The exact boundary, assessor ID, match method and the coordinates used. A nearby match stays marked as nearby.
Districts and additional rules
Each base district and the geometry affecting the tract. Commercial overlays and special districts have their own records.
Which rules are in effect
The source map, ordinance section, effective date and any recent amendment. Keep a vendor’s refresh time in a separate field.
Proposed use
The local use classification and the approval process for the operation. A zoning district label alone leaves those questions open.
Site capacity
The zoning lot used in the calculation and any split-district rules, setbacks, height limits or approvals that change the result.

blocks.text: New York City defines a zoning lot separately from a tax lot. A zoning lot can include multiple lots of record under specified conditions. The city also has separate provisions when a zoning lot crosses district boundaries. Confirm the zoning lot and ask for a written determination when a lease, construction budget or loan depends on the result.

faqs.question: Can I get zoning by address from an API?
faqs.answer: Yes. Some APIs accept an address, then return the district at the matched point or a summary tied to the parcel. Ask which result you are getting and run a polygon check on split lots.

faqs.question: Why does one parcel have several zoning districts?
faqs.answer: A mapped district boundary can cross a tax lot. A polygon overlay returns the intersecting districts and their shares. A parcel summary may omit small intersections under its published reporting rules.

faqs.question: Can I estimate buildable floor area from a zoning API?
faqs.answer: Use the API to screen a scenario. Verify the zoning lot, current rules, intended use and applicable approvals before applying a floor-area figure to a design or project budget.

title: EV charging station APIs for location and live availability
description: Compare AFDC, TomTom, HERE, Google Places and OCPI. Use two Ohio fast-charging stops to test port counts, connector compatibility and live status.
coverAlt: Aerial map of the I-70 and U.S. Route 42 interchange near London, Ohio, with Pilot 454 and TA London marked.
coverCaption: I-70 Exit 79 near London, Ohio. Pins use AFDC station coordinates. Aerial imagery from USGS, USDA and The National Map.
intro: Use the U.S. Department of Energy’s AFDC API to locate charging stations and count installed ports. For a driver who needs a free connector now, use a timestamped availability feed from a mapping provider or charging network. The difference shows up at one Ohio interchange. The federal inventory lists 16 fast-charging ports across two stops. A routine sum of the equipment export returns 160 because it repeats the station total on each row.
takeaways: Count installed ports once per station ID. Preserve repeated equipment rows when the source supplies no equipment ID.
Keep connector compatibility, station access hours and live equipment status in separate fields.
Ask when the network observed the status. A station record can be updated today and still carry no occupancy data.

sections.heading: Which EV charging API should you use?

blocks.text: Start with the decision you need to support. A planner can use an inventory to find gaps in a corridor. A routing app needs to know whether a compatible charger is free and how recently that was observed. The commercial comparisons below use provider documentation. We queried the AFDC feeds for the Ohio example.

rows: U.S. DOE AFDC
U.S. station inventory with public access, location, connector types and installed DC fast port counts. An equipment CSV adds connector counts and rated power.
Check how station counts repeat across equipment rows and whether the station ID survives a refresh.
TomTom
Charging availability grouped by connector type and power. TomTom documents a three-minute refresh for dynamic data.
Check that both networks appear on your corridor. Measure the age of the underlying status and ask how the feed represents unknown availability.
HERE
Place search with optional connector availability, grouped by type and power. The documentation also covers equipment-level status and operator IDs.
Ask which networks expose equipment detail and usable update timestamps on your routes.
Google Places
Place records with EV connector counts and, where available, compatible-group availability, out-of-service counts and an update time.
Check how often the availability fields populate for the places you serve. Google documents how several connectors can share one charger.
Operator feed via OCPI
Operator-provided Locations, EVSEs and Connectors. The OCPI Locations module defines EVSE status and update fields.
Confirm partner access and keep the country, party, location and equipment IDs needed to match updates.

sections.heading: Two Ohio charging stops expose a 10× counting error

blocks.text: We queried AFDC for electric stations in ZIP 43140 and kept the two public locations with DC fast charging. Both sit at I-70 Exit 79. The equipment export below was captured on November 23, 2026 at 07:31 UTC. It reports equipment inventory and rated output.

rows: Pilot Travel Center 454 · 322368
Four identical rows, each listing one CCS connector rated at 350 kW. Each repeats the station count of 4.
Seven rows list one CCS connector and five list one J3400 connector. All list a 400 kW rating and repeat the station count of 12.

blocks.text: Summing the station field over the equipment rows gives 4 × 4 + 12 × 12 = 160. Counting one station total per AFDC ID gives 4 + 12 = 16. Dropping duplicate-looking CSV rows would also lose equipment detail. The four Pilot rows are identical in the export. AFDC allows an equipment row to describe more than one port or connector, so keep the three quantities separate in your data model.

The Pilot stop also shows why the kW field needs its own label. Ohio’s opening announcement gave a maximum of 350 kW for a single vehicle, with up to 175 kW per port during simultaneous use. Keep the equipment rating for compatibility filters and use a separately sourced power curve or measured data for charging-time estimates.

blocks.label: Download the Ohio station records and port-count audit

sections.heading: Test the answer a driver will see

blocks.text: Suppose a driver with a J3400 inlet wants to stop at TA London. The AFDC export identifies five J3400 connectors there. The station has status E and reports 24-hour public access. That is enough to show a candidate stop. To say how many compatible chargers are free, match the station to a live feed, read the status for the compatible equipment, and retain its update time.

rows: A recent observation with compatible equipment free
Show the count, when it was observed and which connector type it covers.
A recent observation with zero free
Show that no compatible chargers are free. Distinguish ones in use from ones out of service when the feed does.
An old observation
Show when the status was last checked and offer another stop. Set the cutoff using observed delay on that network.
No status, an unknown value, or an unmatched station
Show that live status is unavailable. Keep the inventory and access hours visible.

blocks.text: For the trial, run these two station IDs and add locations from every network you expect customers to use. Compare the API with the operator’s view at the same times over a week. Log whether each station matched, whether it had a timestamp, and how old the observation was when your app received it. Include a known outage and a station with several connectors sharing one charger. Those cases reveal whether the feed can support a routing decision.

sections.heading: Use surrounding land and road data for expansion decisions

blocks.text: For network planning, this inventory can show where fast charging is concentrated. Invariant Earth supplies surrounding parcel and road context, including nearest major road name, road class and distance. A truck corridor study also needs the entrance location, usable turning geometry, and a route that fits the vehicle and trailer. Take a proposed load and operating schedule to the serving utility when evaluating a new site.

faqs.question: Does the AFDC API show current EV charger availability?
faqs.answer: The AFDC station status describes the facility. Use the AFDC inventory to find stations and installed ports, then use a live operator or aggregator feed for occupancy.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a charging station, an EVSE and a connector?
faqs.answer: A station is a site with charging equipment. In OCPI, one EVSE can charge one vehicle at a time. A connector is the plug or socket on that equipment. An EVSE can offer several connector types.

faqs.question: How do I count public DC fast-charging ports from AFDC?
faqs.answer: Filter electric stations by public access and DC fast charging, then sum the installed DC fast port count once per station ID. Keep equipment rows for connector detail and use a status feed for the current free count.

title: Geoforge alternatives for data center power screening
description: Compare Geoforge, Paces, PVcase, GridCARE and Invariant. Use 49 PJM upgrade records to test the dates and assumptions behind a data center power forecast.
coverAlt: Illustrative aerial view of transmission towers and a construction lane crossing harvested fields.
coverCaption: AI-generated illustration of a transmission corridor in agricultural terrain.
intro: Geoforge is a starting point for comparing potential connections and modeled offtake. Consider Paces for screening a portfolio, PVcase Prospect for checking grid constraints, GridCARE where the utility is evaluating flexible load, or Invariant for a study tied to a particular campus ramp. Give every provider the same test. Ask which upgrade puts power within reach, which date the report uses, and how the first phase changes when the upgrade moves.
takeaways: In one PJM plan, the same 765 kV line segment had a June 2030 required date and an October 2031 projected date, a gap of 517 days.
AEP Ohio used separate service estimates for different groups of studied customers. One group needed an additional regional upgrade.
A usable power forecast names the connection, the case year, the limiting element and the work required for each load phase.

sections.heading: Which Geoforge alternative fits your site search?

blocks.text: The table summarizes public product descriptions. Use the Ohio example below to test what a provider can explain about its output for your location.

columns: What to ask in the demo
rows: Geoforge
Site reports with potential connections, modeled offtake by year and scenario, queue context and an energization estimate. It also offers deeper power-flow studies.
Ask which grid case and upgrade records drive the range for the first phase. Request the basis for any competing load in that case.
Paces
Regional capacity screening, project-level connection evaluation and support through interconnection studies.
Ask how capacity layer results carry into a study of your site, and which grid, land or permitting issue changes the shortlist.
PVcase Prospect
Modeled injection and withdrawal, with limiting elements for different scenarios. The published documentation distinguishes base-case and contingency coverage by market.
Check the available scenarios for your region and whether the constraint is already present before your load is added.
GridCARE
Utility work on grid capacity for flexible loads. National Grid describes its use in New York and work with UK Electricity Transmission.
Confirm the serving utility is involved and get the MW, hours, operating limits and dispatch conditions for any flexible service.
Invariant
The published site-study workflow covers AC power flow, contingency analysis, candidate connections, and indicative costs and timing.
Request the case vintage, phased results and limiting facilities. Ask which assumptions can be rerun as utility evidence changes.

sections.heading: An Ohio power forecast can contain several valid dates

blocks.text: AEP Ohio’s November 2025 study letter covered about 13 GW of new data center load. It found that the studied projects needed regional transmission work under the scenarios evaluated. Its initial estimate was Q4 2031 for Clusters 1 and 3 with the regional project and applicable parallel upgrades in service. Cluster 2 had a 2033 planning estimate and needed another regional solution. A buyer needs the customer’s actual service plan to determine which work applies.

PJM cross-references the first regional proposal, 2025W1-570, to upgrade package b4068. In the March 2026 assessment, b4068.2, the AEP portion of the Greentown to Teddy 765 kV line, had a required date of June 1, 2030 and a projected date of October 31, 2031. The first is the planning need date. The second is the forecast in that report. A particular customer’s electric service date has its own evidence.

rows: Planning need for b4068.2
June 1, 2030
Keep it as the date the reliability plan requires the work.
Projected in-service date for b4068.2
October 31, 2031
Use it as a dated component forecast and check the latest schedule.
AEP Ohio Cluster 2 service planning estimate
Check the second regional dependency, local work and actual customer schedule.

blocks.text: AEP Ohio later reported that 5,642 MW had signed binding contracts under the new tariff as of February 12, 2026. That update gives the scale of the committed cohort. It leaves the distribution by bus, year and cluster open. Ask your provider how it treats unconfirmed demand, then test a scenario with a different set of competing projects.

sections.heading: What the 49 PJM upgrade rows show

blocks.text: We extracted the required and projected dates for each b4068 sub-ID in the March assessment. Two rows projected June 2028, 21 projected October 2030, and 26 projected October 2031. These are counts of published sub-IDs. A project forecast should identify the subset the connection actually depends on.

Two rows in that assessment show an invalid calendar value in the required-date column. The February board recommendations show June 1, 2030 for both sub-IDs. The download retains the February dates and the March source values separately, with the latter normalized to null. Ask a provider which source its model used and how it handles this sort of discrepancy.

sections.heading: How to test the first phase before paying for a site option

blocks.text: Give the vendor the parcel, the minimum load needed on day one, the full facility load, the two service dates and how much load you can curtail. For example, ask for 50 MW by July 2030 and 200 MW by January 2032 at the meter. Those are illustrative targets, with the utility service for your project to be confirmed.

items: Ask for the modeled MW on each date at the same connection point. Record the model year, the limiting equipment and the outage assumption.
Request a second run with the relevant upgrade out of service through your target date. Ask which phase remains feasible and what changes the answer.
Get the utility’s written service terms, required work and estimated start of service. Keep energization and facility handover as separate milestones.

faqs.question: What are the best Geoforge alternatives for finding power for a data center?
faqs.answer: Consider Paces for portfolio screening, PVcase Prospect for modeled point-of-interconnection constraints, GridCARE for opportunities that depend on utility-supported load flexibility, and Invariant for a phased site study. Test your actual service dates with each provider.

faqs.question: What is the difference between required and projected in-service dates?
faqs.answer: The required date expresses when the planning case needs an upgrade. The projected date is the schedule estimate in that record. PJM’s March 2026 assessment lists June 1, 2030 and October 31, 2031 respectively for b4068.2. Use the relevant utility agreement and construction schedule to evaluate customer service.

faqs.question: Can a power screening report tell me when I can energize a data center?
faqs.answer: A power screen can estimate when the grid could support a proposed load under a specific case. The serving utility’s agreement and work plan establish the commercial service terms and estimated date. Confirm energization through a commissioning or utility record.

title: Ageospatial alternatives for commercial roof underwriting
description: Compare Ageospatial, Moody’s, ZestyAI, Verisk and Invariant Earth with a real test for building identity, roof replacement dates and source evidence.
coverAlt: Aerial view of the Rosemead Public Works warehouse with its county building footprint outlined.
coverCaption: 2022 USDA NAIP imagery via CDFW. The outline marks the building identified on the city site map. The photo predates the 2025 roof work.
intro: Ageospatial is worth evaluating when underwriters need to match insured buildings and collect evidence from imagery, maps and records. Moody’s, ZestyAI and Verisk offer dedicated roof products. Invariant Earth fits teams assembling their own property data workflow. To compare them, start with a submission that has two addresses and three different dates for the same roof project.
takeaways: Compare products on the exact building and roof scope. The owner’s mailing address can point to a different property.
A replacement project has an award date, a completion date and a date when the evidence became available to your team. Keep all three.
A roof age estimate, a report of completed work and a current condition rating answer different underwriting questions.

sections.heading: Which Ageospatial alternative fits your workflow?

blocks.text: Decide what the underwriter needs to do with the answer. An inspection team may need a roof and imagery report. A quoting team may need a structured age field with a confidence signal. A data team may need the building match, its source and a way to store later corrections. The comparison below uses public product descriptions. The municipal records provide an independent case you can run with each vendor.

columns: What to ask for in a trial
rows: Ageospatial
Workflow examples tie a submission line to the parcel and footprint, show a dated roof image, and flag changes and nearby exposures.
Have the tool link each finding to the original record. Export the resolved building, both addresses and the dates behind the replacement finding.
Moody’s Commercial Property Intelligence
Commercial building and roof data, including imagery-derived age and condition, with API, batch and application delivery.
Ask what drove the age estimate for the selected commercial roof and whether the output can show a date range or leave the age open.
ZestyAI Roof Age
Roof replacement estimates from imagery and permit records, with confidence and modeled values where direct evidence is sparse. ZestyAI describes use in a commercial portfolio.
Ask how the model distinguishes a full replacement from partial work and which fields expose the evidence or model basis.
Verisk Roof Underwriting Report
A commercial roof report with age, condition, material, equipment and an estimated roof replacement cost.
Review the target location and scope of the reported age and cost. Ask what can be retained as machine-readable data.
Invariant Earth
A coordinate-based API with fields for the primary building footprint area, height, floor count and class where supported.
Use the field catalog to choose the spatial inputs. Establish the roof event from the city record and retain it alongside the matched building in your workflow.

sections.heading: The Rosemead test starts with two addresses

blocks.text: Rosemead’s July 2025 notice attachment gives 8838 E Valley Boulevard as the city’s address and 2714 River Avenue as the location where the roof work took place. The project documents identify the Public Works Office and Warehouse Building at the River Avenue site. The site map on page TP-1 points to that building among several neighboring roofs.

Even the correct street address can produce different coordinates. The Census Geocoder returned an address-range coordinate that intersects no outline in the county’s 2023 building layer. The county address point was about 64 meters away, carried assessor parcel ID 5282026900 and intersected county outline 2920695. The outline matches the building shape pointed to on the city’s map. The county address record itself has a blank building ID.

That matters in a coordinate-based API. Invariant Earth describes its primary footprint field as using the enclosing Overture building or searching within 100 meters for the nearest one. Keep the input coordinates and review the returned match against the project map before using the result in the file. The county outline in the aerial cover is shown for identification. The photograph is from 2022.

sections.heading: When did the roof actually change?

rows: January 14, 2025
The city awarded the roof replacement contract.
A named project and planned scope.
June 2, 2025
Completion date stated in the notice attachment in the July packet.
The reported date of the replacement work and the later source document date.
July 8, 2025
The council accepted the work and authorized recording the notice.
The acceptance action and authority to record. The county recording date remains unverified.

blocks.text: The staff report says the old metal roofing system was removed and a new metal system installed. The final project cost included additional cooler work. Store that amount as project expenditure and request a cost breakdown or a separate estimate when you need the replacement cost of the roof alone.

For a hypothetical June 30 quote supported only by the records dated by then, keep the replacement completion field open. At a July 31 review with the July packet in hand, add the reported June 2 completion as a new piece of evidence and keep the prior quote snapshot. A dated inspection would answer a separate question about the roof’s current condition.

faqs.question: What are alternatives to Ageospatial for commercial property underwriting?
faqs.answer: Compare Moody’s for imagery-derived commercial building and roof data, ZestyAI for roof age and confidence, Verisk for a commercial roof report, and Invariant Earth for coordinate-based data in a workflow you control. faqs.question: Can I verify a commercial roof replacement by address?
faqs.answer: Use the property address to identify the building, then verify the roof scope and completion date against a closeout, inspection, warranty or comparable record. At Rosemead the site and owner address were different, and the city’s June 2 completion date appeared in the July packet.

faqs.question: Is the roof replacement date the same as the council acceptance date?
faqs.answer: The two dates describe different events. In Rosemead, the notice lists June 2, 2025 as the completion date, and the council accepted the work on July 8, 2025.

title: West Kite Alternatives for Commercial Property Data
description: Compare West Kite, ATTOM, Regrid, and Invariant Earth. Use a 25 Water Street case to test address matching, unit counts, permits, and occupancy history.
coverAlt: 2024 aerial photograph of 25 Water Street in Lower Manhattan with its tax lot outlined and a construction crane on the roof.
coverCaption: 25 Water Street during conversion. Cropped NYC OTI 2024 aerial imagery, CC BY 4.0. Invariant added the MapPLUTO 26v2 tax lot outline.
intro: Try West Kite for commercial property records and owner research, ATTOM for property and transaction data in a workflow you already run, and Regrid for parcel identity and boundaries. Evaluate Invariant Earth when you need sourced site conditions alongside a parcel match. To choose among them, give each provider a building that changed use and ask it to reconstruct what happened. At 25 Water Street, a property lookup and the city’s occupancy records give different unit totals for the same conversion.
takeaways: West Kite’s public lookup resolved three addresses to the same property and returned 1,323 units. MapPLUTO reports 1,323 total units and 1,320 residential units on that lot.
DOB NOW has four issuances of the same general construction permit and ten occupancy issuance records under the related job. Keep each event and its date.
Ask a provider which entity and source each field describes, and whether a historical query retrieves what was known at the time of a decision.

sections.heading: Which property API fits the job?

blocks.text: Invariant makes Invariant Earth. We reviewed the providers’ public documentation and ran the West Kite unauthenticated address lookup on November 22, 2026. The other rows describe documented capabilities and give tests for a paid trial.

rows: West Kite
Commercial property records, ownership research, sales, assessments, and permits.
Resolve address aliases and request the permit sequence and original sources. Check whether an occupancy certificate is available for the exact building and date.
ATTOM
Property characteristics, deeds, mortgages, sales and building permits for an integration.
Use the same address and assessor ID. Confirm county coverage and ask which permit dates and identifiers the feed exposes.
Regrid
Parcel boundaries, assessor IDs, and matching across county records.
Verify how the current and prior parcel versions link after a split or merger. Join building and permit records from their issuing agencies.
Invariant Earth

title: Mireye Alternatives for U.S. Property Screening
description: Compare Mireye, Invariant Earth, West Kite, and Regrid for U.S. property screening. Check how each handles parcel matches, hazards, and utility evidence.
coverAlt: Illustrative aerial view of an industrial building beside winding wetlands.
coverCaption: AI-generated illustration of an industrial site beside wetlands.
intro: For a Mireye alternative, start with what you need to screen. Try Invariant Earth when your workflow needs source-backed location fields and a visible parcel match. Try West Kite when you need a report that measures flood and wetland overlap across a lot. Try Regrid when the parcel boundary and identifier are the main records you need. Keep Mireye in the evaluation when you want public location fields and a separate parcel-enrichment workflow.
takeaways: Compare the coordinates and geometry behind each field. The same field name can describe a different search or source.
Both Mireye and Invariant use wetland_acres for an entire selected wetland polygon. To estimate affected acreage, calculate its intersection with the property or project area.
Bring the same assessor parcel, hazard map and required service level to each trial. Record the provider’s matching, missing data and source dates.

sections.heading: Which tool should you evaluate?

blocks.text: Invariant makes Invariant Earth. We reviewed public catalogs and documentation on November 22, 2026. The comparison describes documented inputs and outputs. Test account-specific coverage, latency, and results on your own properties.

columns: What to check in a trial
rows: Mireye
Point data through Fetch or parcel records through Enrich.
Compare the input coordinate with Enrich’s analysis_point. Its documented example resolves a parcel and uses the stored parcel centroid for analysis.
Invariant Earth
Location and parcel fields with field-level source, dataset vintage and status.
Inspect parcel_match_type and parcel_match_distance_m. The parcel ID can fall back to a nearest parcel within 250 meters. Check the match before joining another dataset.
West Kite
Commercial property research and a report using the parcel outline for flood and wetland area.
Check the property match and whether each layer is published for the county. The documented response identifies fields that could not be answered.
Regrid
Parcel IDs and boundaries for use in your own GIS or pipeline.
Use the county record to verify a recent split. Regrid explains which events preserve its ID and which retire it.

sections.heading: Four fields to verify before switching

blocks.text: Mireye publishes separate catalogs for Fetch and Enrich. Invariant lists parcel-match fields in its location catalog. Check the catalog for the endpoint that will serve the workflow. The download records the field name, published unit, source identifier, and what to verify for each output.

rows: Is the location in a mapped flood zone?
Both document within_floodplain_polygon as a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area test at a point.
For land or buildings, intersect the full geometry with the effective FEMA polygons. Keep the map date and area by zone.
How many wetland acres affect the tract?
Both define wetland_acres as the total area of the selected National Wetlands Inventory polygon. It can be the nearest wetland, including one outside the tract.
Intersect mapped wetlands with the tax lot or proposed disturbance area, then calculate the acreage inside it.
Which substation should we investigate?
Both expose nearest_substation_distance_m. Invariant lists a 10 km search. Mireye describes an EIA layer for substations at 69 kV or above.
Save the returned facility, layer and method. Confirm the serving utility and proposed connection before relying on a capacity estimate.
How reliable is the water service map?
Both expose water_service_area_provenance. Invariant describes the boundary method and original provider. Mireye describes source-based and modeled categories.
Save the original evidence. Ask the utility about pressure, flow, and a service commitment for the intended use.

Request the parcel boundary separately and record where each result was evaluated. Include a multi-parcel site in the trial when that is part of your usual work.

Use the same source layer and edition when reconciling values. At Brooklyn Army Terminal, for example, the published location point returned FEMA Zone AE. Save the field status with the value. Mireye Fetch and Invariant Earth document a distinction between a successful value, no data at a location, and a failed field request. A successful response can include a failed field. Store the dataset edition separately from the fetch time, especially when you are recreating an earlier decision.

title: How to Check Wildfire Risk by Address for Commercial Property
description: Match the right building, verify the wildfire map and its date, and document what needs inspection. Includes two reproducible Los Angeles address checks.
coverAlt: Illustration of a commercial building at the edge of dry Southern California hills.
coverCaption: Illustration of a fictional site. The Los Angeles checks below use public map records.
intro: Start with the building on the submission. Match its address to a footprint, check which wildfire map applies, and save the map result with the source and date. At Griffith Observatory, two county address points for the same facility are about 33 meters apart. The two points return the same hazard category. Only one intersects the mapped building. The location check is useful even when the zone result agrees.
takeaways: Keep the matched building ID and the way the address was located. A street point can return a valid map category for the wrong building.
Keep the published hazard category, map edition and source record. A mapped NonWildland result is different from missing coverage.
Request current evidence for the roof, vents, nearby combustibles and access before evaluating the building’s susceptibility to wildfire.

sections.heading: Match the address to the building on the submission

blocks.text: Use the street address, ZIP code and building or suite identifier to find candidate locations. At a commercial campus, check the building on the statement of values, which lists the locations and amounts submitted for insurance. Confirm the address against an owner-provided site plan or other building record. Keep each building as its own record when several structures share a parcel or mailing address. County address datasets can contain multiple source points and omit some units.

Record whether the location came from a building, parcel, street segment or ZIP code. A point that falls inside a building is stronger evidence than a street estimate. Review the footprint’s source date and compare it with current records for additions, replacements or multiple structures at the same address.

blocks.text: We matched the facilities’ published addresses to county address points and building outlines, then queried the complete polygons against the State Fire Marshal’s 2025 recommended layer for Local Responsibility Areas. Both buildings were within a single mapped class. The county outlines report 2008 source imagery with an Unchanged status in the queried service.

The city’s separate Very High zone layer also matched the Observatory footprint and returned no intersection for the library. Confirm the locally applicable map and its effective date with the jurisdiction for any dated decision.

sections.heading: Save the map version and the relationship to the zone

blocks.text: California’s Fire Hazard Severity Zones describe long-term hazard using vegetation, terrain, fire weather and other factors. To find the map for an address, start with the responsibility area. CAL FIRE publishes State Responsibility Area maps, and the State Fire Marshal provides recommended Local Responsibility Area zones. Ask the local jurisdiction which map was in effect on your decision date. Record the publisher, layer, version, effective date where verified, retrieval date and original class.

Compare the full building outline with every intersecting polygon. Keep the classes and whether the building is inside, crosses a boundary, or only touches its edge. Route uncertain matches and mixed footprints for review, especially when a source point or older footprint can change the result. Keep the raw response so the decision can be reviewed after the source updates.

For portfolios outside California, start with the applicable state or local source. The U.S. Forest Service’s Wildfire Risk to Communities data can help prioritize regions to investigate. The Forest Service describes it as a community-scale resource and cautions against using it at the individual-property scale.

sections.heading: What to keep in the underwriting file

blocks.text: Use public mapping to document exposure and direct the next review. The California Department of Insurance describes CAL FIRE’s severity maps as planning tools and explains that insurers use separate wildfire risk models for underwriting and pricing. Keep the map result beside the carrier’s distinct model result and version, where your workflow uses one.

Submitted address, building ID, match method, footprint date and unresolved matches.
Owner’s building schedule or a site plan when a parcel contains more than one structure.
Mapped hazard
Publisher, map version, date, zone label, footprint relation and any coverage gap.

Perimeter source, data version, time period and relationship to the building.
Inspection, repair or loss records for questions about damage to a specific structure.
Building susceptibility
Roof covering and condition, vents, openings, vegetation, combustible storage and access.
Dated inspection, photographs or maintenance records that identify the building and conditions reviewed.
Insurance decision
Which evidence informed the referral, unresolved questions, and the carrier’s applicable terms or model output.
Carrier guidance and the applicable policy or binder.

blocks.text: A historical perimeter indicates a mapped past event. CAL FIRE describes gaps and generalization in those records, including areas inside a perimeter that may have escaped burning. A building intersection is a reason to check loss or inspection records. For the condition review, IBHS’s commercial guidance identifies components worth examining, including roofs, vents and nearby combustible material.

sections.heading: Which commercial property policies does SB 547 cover?

blocks.text: California Insurance Code section 675.55 applies to eligible commercial property policies already in force at the time of the emergency declaration. The one-year protection concerns cancellation or nonrenewal based solely on the structure’s location in an area where a wildfire occurred. Section 675.1 addresses residential policies.

For ordinary commercial property, the size exclusion requires both an annual premium of at least $25,000 and an average of at least 25 employees in the preceding 12 months. The statute overrides that size exclusion for policies covering loss or damage to real property used primarily for commercial residential or habitational purposes, such as apartment complexes and qualifying association property. Inland marine, transit and transportation policies are separately excluded. Section 675.55(b) sets out additional exceptions.

sections.heading: A renewal in ZIP code 95370

blocks.text: ZIP code 95370 appears in both bulletins. Suppose a commercial property policy for a building there first took effect October 1, 2026. It was in force on the Dove declaration date and began after the Gann declaration date. Bring the Dove bulletin into the review and record the policy inception date alongside both matches. The reviewer still needs the policy type, applicable exclusions and the insurer’s stated reason.

For notices that meet the bulletin’s conditions, the Department directs insurers to offer to rescind wildfire-related cancellation or nonrenewal notices and offer reinstatement or renewal. A policyholder can ask the carrier to review the notice against the applicable bulletin and contact the Department for assistance when needed.

items: Save the insured address and ZIP from the policy schedule, with the bulletin number and source page. Keep one record per fire and ZIP so overlapping events remain visible.
Record the declaration date, bulletin issue date, policy effective date, notice date, notice reason and proposed end date.
For commercial property, capture the policy form and principal use, and record the annual premium and average employment when the statutory exclusion requires them.
Route conflicting dates, uncertain address matches and policies covering multiple locations for review with the supporting records.

blocks.text: The Department distinguishes CAL FIRE’s Fire Hazard Severity Zone maps, used for planning, from insurers’ wildfire risk models. The bulletin ZIP list answers a separate question about which areas the agency identified for a specific renewal protection.

title: How to verify a shovel-ready industrial site
description: See what industrial site certification covers and verify buildable land, power, water, wastewater and permits. Compare two certified Tennessee sites.
coverAlt: Two certified Tennessee sites compared against an example requirement of 25 developable acres and 3 million gallons per day of water system headroom.
coverCaption: Published figures for the Canterbury and I-40 Advantage sites against an illustrative screen. Water figures refer to the system’s reported excess capacity.
intro: A shovel-ready designation tells you what a site program reviewed. To decide whether a factory can start on schedule, check the exact tract, the accepted land use, the usable acreage and the utilities that can commit to the project. Two sites in the same Tennessee certification announcement illustrate the difference. One clears the example acreage requirement. The other clears the initial water screen.
takeaways: Keep the certifying program, date and tract boundary with the designation.
Compare usable site area with the latest layout and keep related acreage figures tied to their original boundaries.
Ask each provider for a service offer at the proposed connection point, including the project’s volume, required upgrades and delivery date.
Publish an evidence date and a next action for every open constraint in the inventory.

sections.heading: What shovel-ready certification covers

blocks.text: Select Tennessee’s published criteria call for at least 20 developable acres, truck-quality access, documented site conditions and utilities onsite or a formal extension plan. The program accepts current zoning or an expedited rezoning plan. Those are meaningful signals to start with. For a buyer, the difference between an installed connection and an extension plan can be months of work.

Read the actual program rules when comparing badges. Kentucky’s separate Build-Ready designation builds on its shovel-ready criteria and requires a completed, engineer-certified pad for a building of at least 50,000 square feet, with room to expand to at least 100,000. The building pad and its expansion area are distinct from the gross tract acreage.

The state’s public listings report different combinations of acreage, zoning and utility characteristics. The table uses the public records as reviewed on November 22, 2026. blocks.text: Suppose a manufacturer needs at least 25 contiguous developable acres and 3 million gallons per day (MGD) of water. Canterbury’s listed 24 developable acres are below the acreage requirement. Brownsville’s listed 154 developable acres clear the numerical acreage screen, subject to a layout and contiguity check. Its 2.5 MGD of reported system excess water capacity is below the initial water screen. The public figures leave a blocker at each site. For a live decision, ask the water provider what it can actually commit to at the parcel, including flow and pressure at peak demand.

The equal 161 kV entries describe voltage at the substation. To compare deliverable electric service, request MW, voltage at the meter, reliability, deposit and upgrade requirements, and the service date. At Brownsville, TVA completed a June 2025 environmental review of proposed work on 110 acres, including clearing, grading for a dirt pad and rerouting a gravel road. That report follows the September 2024 certification announcement. Ask for the dated as-built pad certification or survey to establish what work is in place for the tract being offered.

title: How to check FEMA flood zone history for commercial property underwriting
description: Check which FEMA flood map applied on a quote or loan date. Use building footprints, effective dates and map revision records to audit commercial flood exposure.
coverAlt: Current FEMA map zones within the Huntington revision area, beside a timeline of the July 2021 issue date, December 2021 effective date and January 2024 Alexandria panel.
coverCaption: Current FEMA flood zones inside the Huntington revision boundary. The revision took effect in December 2021 and FEMA later incorporated it into a revised Alexandria panel.
intro: To check a commercial building’s FEMA flood zone on a past date, match the insured building to its footprint, find the map panel effective on that date and apply any map changes that were already in force. Save the map and change records with the decision. An address-only lookup against today’s National Flood Hazard Layer gives you a current result and can miss the history that mattered on the quote date.
takeaways: Record the insured building, map panel and effective date, applicable FEMA case number, and when the result was retrieved.
Track issue dates, effective dates and later panel publication separately. A single FEMA revision can have all three.
Keep mapped flood zones, modeled depth, expected loss and any required lender determination in separate fields.
Send ambiguous building matches, boundary touches and missing historic maps to review rather than counting them as outside the hazard area.

sections.heading: Match the building before you look up the zone

blocks.text: Start with a stable building ID and the insured location or collateral schedule. Confirm which structures belong to the account and retain the geometry that supports each match. A mailing address may resolve to a driveway, parcel centroid or neighboring building. On a multi-building site, two structures can have different map results even though they share an address.

Intersect each confirmed footprint with the map polygons. Preserve zone code, zone subtype and the Special Flood Hazard Area flag. Record boundary contact separately from an area overlap. Where the footprint, map or positional accuracy leaves the outcome uncertain, record the exception for review. Do not silently assign all the buildings on the parcel to the zone at its address pin.

sections.heading: Find the map that applied on the decision date

rows: Effective map panel

Preliminary or pending maps
Map status and publication date. Use for forward-looking review. For the effective-map result, use the adopted panel and applicable effective changes.
Retrieval evidence
Retrieval time, source URL and a preserved response or file identifier. A map made effective in 2021 may only have been retrieved by your team in 2026.

blocks.text: FEMA’s Map Service Center provides historic and effective map products. The National Flood Hazard Layer, or NFHL, is useful for current effective GIS data. FEMA’s separate Flood Map Changes Viewer also shows preliminary and pending layers, which FEMA describes as information for review and awareness.

Retain both the date a map change took effect and the date you obtained it. That lets a reviewer distinguish a replay against the best available historical source from a replay of the records actually on file when the decision was made. Keep the historical match geometry and its own vintage, too.

blocks.text: Fairfax County reports that the Cameron Run levee revision removed the levee-protected area in Huntington, Virginia, from the Special Flood Hazard Area. title: Best GIS APIs for U.S. site selection
description: Compare GIS APIs for parcels, zoning, flood exposure, and power screening. Test the difference between a location pin and a parcel with a real site.
coverAlt: Aerial map of Brooklyn Army Terminal with the shoreline-clipped tax lot outlined in white, Zone AE on the lot shaded blue, and the published coordinate marked just outside the boundary.
coverCaption: Brooklyn Army Terminal. The white outline is the MapPLUTO 26v2 tax lot, blue shows FEMA Zone AE within it, and the gold dot marks the published coordinate. Aerial imagery from NYS ITS, spring 2024.
intro: For U.S. site selection, start with the evidence your team needs to keep or rule out a site. Evaluate Regrid for parcel identity, West Kite for commercial property records, and Esri for mapping and routing. Evaluate Invariant Earth or Mireye when a screening workflow needs cited terrain, hazards, and nearby infrastructure. For a large electrical load, also compare project-level studies from Invariant and screening products such as Geoforge or Paces.
takeaways: Test the exact counties and fields where you plan to operate. A national map can still have uneven coverage for permits, zoning, or owner data.
A site pin, a tax lot, and a proposed building can return different hazard results. Ask which geometry an API evaluated.
For every decision-critical field, keep the source, observation date, and status alongside the value.

sections.heading: Which provider fits the job?

blocks.text: Invariant makes Invariant Earth. The comparison below uses public product documentation reviewed on November 22, 2026. The Brooklyn example is our own calculation from city and federal data. We did not run an authenticated comparison of all providers, so the table describes documented capabilities and what to verify.

rows: Esri ArcGIS Location Platform
Geocoding, basemaps, routing, and publishing spatial layers.
Check how geocodes resolve on large campuses. Confirm that the plan supports storing geocodes and serving your own data layers.
Regrid
Parcel boundaries and identifiers, APN lookups, and bulk property enrichment.
Test a recent parcel split, then check county refresh dates and coverage for zoning, building footprints, and matched addresses.
West Kite
Commercial property research across owners, deeds, assessments, permits, and site context.
Start with its county-level coverage. Test whether the deed, permit, or mortgage that matters to your team is available for the exact property.
Mireye
Location enrichment and screening with source information across land, hazards, and infrastructure.
Ask for the source, spatial method, and missing-value behavior for the same point and parcel. Check which tools accept a polygon.
Invariant Earth
Combining location and parcel fields with source links, dataset vintages, and field-level status.
Fetch fields for a known coordinate. Check how matching works near parcel boundaries and whether each field supports the time period you need.
Geoforge
Shareable power screening reports with modeled load and generation headroom, queue context, and planned upgrades.
Check the study year, load direction, and assumptions for each candidate connection. Ask how you can export the data behind the report.
Paces
Finding and screening data center sites with power and development constraints in one workflow.
Ask for a shortlist using your phased load and service dates. Verify how the workflow handles utility feedback, site control, and evidence for each milestone.
PVcase Prospect
Map-based site screening, with withdrawal capacity studies for data center loads.
Check which connection, load case, and study year the capacity layer represents. Verify the site and power questions that still need utility evidence.
Ageospatial
Property and infrastructure intelligence for insurance and credit workflows.
Give it a schedule with multiple buildings at one address. Inspect the evidence behind the building match and risk inputs.

sections.heading: A real parcel test at Brooklyn Army Terminal

blocks.text: For Brooklyn Army Terminal tax lot 3057780001, FEMA returned Zone AE at the coordinate published in MapPLUTO. The point was about 9 meters outside the shoreline-clipped tax lot. When we intersected the lot itself with the same FEMA layer, 19.9% of its area was in Zone AE and 80.1% was in Zone X. Zone X within this lot includes both the 0.2% annual chance hazard area and the area FEMA maps as minimal hazard.

We queried NYC MapPLUTO 26v2 by borough, block, and lot, then pulled FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer polygons from layer 28 around the lot. We projected the geometry to UTM zone 18N, intersected and grouped the polygons by FEMA zone and subtype, and divided each overlap by the clipped parcel area. The calculation uses mapped land area. For a particular structure, run the intersection again on its building footprint. The downloadable file contains the exact source queries, coordinate, lot, and clipped zone geometry.

sections.heading: Run the same checks before you sign

blocks.text: Give each vendor the same three inputs. Use a tract whose county record you have in hand, a parcel that recently split, and a site where a hazard boundary crosses the property. Agree on the reference records and the assessment date before looking at any result.

columns: What you should be able to verify
rows: Parcel match
The returned assessor parcel number and geometry correspond to the tract, including where an address spans multiple parcels.
Owner and date
You can identify the owner of record, the record that supports the result, and the relevant filing or publication date.
Hazard coverage
You can see the exact layer and distinguish a point lookup, a parcel intersection, and a building-footprint intersection.
Infrastructure
You can identify the actual asset, the source and date, and how the distance was measured. A capacity figure comes with a connection point, study case, and project assumptions.
History
You can tell what was known at an earlier decision date, how later corrections are handled, and what happens to identifiers during splits and merges.
Gaps and rights
You can tell an unmatched record from unavailable coverage or a failed request. The license covers how you plan to store and share results.

sections.heading: What Invariant Earth returns

blocks.text: Invariant Earth takes a U.S. coordinate and a list of fields. Its catalog documents fields for parcel matches, terrain, flood context, and nearby grid assets. The response contract includes a source identifier, source link, dataset vintage, and fetched time. A dataset can be republished less often than it is fetched, so keep both dates. Use the coordinate API to build an initial evidence file. For a historical boundary, ask for the exact prior dataset or a working as-of lookup before building around it. title: How to Check Hail History by Address for Commercial Insurance
description: Compare NOAA hail reports and radar estimates at a building. A Denver example shows what a five-kilometer search can tell a commercial underwriter.
coverAlt: Radar map for May 30, 2024 in Denver. Sample points A and B both match a nearby 2.75-inch hail report. Their nearest radar cells show 1.42 and 0.55 inches.
coverCaption: Four-hour peak radar estimates and selected reports for the Denver storm. A and B are sample locations. Source data from NOAA MRMS and NCEI Storm Events.
intro: To check hail history by address, locate the building on the policy or submission. Then search dated hail reports around it and read the radar grid over the building for the same time window. Nearby reports document what was reported at other locations. Radar estimates help decide where to look more closely. Roof condition comes from records or an inspection tied to the building.
takeaways: Keep the matched building, the search radius and the storm time window with the result.
Store the distance and reported hail size separately from the radar estimate at the building.
Record missing radar data and unresolved roof condition explicitly.

sections.heading: Two points in the same Denver hailstorm

blocks.text: On May 30, 2024, severe storms crossed metropolitan Denver. We took two illustrative locations 4.15 km apart and searched the same NOAA hail episode from 8 p.m. to midnight Mountain Daylight Time. For each point we kept records with a published start location and a reported hail size within 5 km. Both searches returned the same 2.75-inch report as their largest. The point nearest that report had a radar estimate of 1.42 inches. The other had a radar estimate of 0.55 inches.

10 records

blocks.text: The radius search describes the neighborhood around each point. The radar product estimates hail size for cells about a kilometer across. The sample uses the nearest grid center without interpolation. For a real address match, identify the building footprint and the relevant roof sections before using either result.

blocks.label: Download the Denver hail evidence and expected results

sections.heading: Check the time zone and the units

blocks.text: Storm Events records the 2.75-inch report start as May 30 at 21:12 with the offset MST-7. That converts to 10:12 p.m. on May 30 in Denver daylight time and 04:12 UTC on May 31. The matching radar window spans 02:00 to 06:00 UTC on May 31. A search restricted to May 30 UTC would miss the evening storm.

The radar product is NOAA’s Maximum Estimated Size of Hail, or MESH. Its 240-minute file stores each cell’s peak estimate for the preceding four hours in millimeters. Divide by 25.4 to compare those values with reports in inches. Keep the timestamp and window length together so a later reader can reproduce the search.

An earlier file ending at 8 p.m. local time returned the raw code −1 for both cells. NOAA lists −1 as missing and −3 as no coverage. Store the numeric estimate as unknown alongside the original code. In the download, each source file has a URL and checksum. The download uses a later version of the bulk archive. For a point-in-time review, use the file version you actually had on the decision date.

Address and building identifier, footprint, geocode precision and match date.
Links the record to the building. A campus address can cover several roofs.
Nearby hail report
Event ID, source category, timestamp and offset, coordinates, hail size and distance.
Documents a report near the building. Report counts can include multiple records from one storm.
Radar estimate
Product, source file, window, cell center, units, estimate or missing code.
Shows modeled exposure near a location during that window and helps prioritize follow-up.
Roof record
Roof section, covering, last verified installation, inspection date and scope of any repair.
Helps establish which roof was present during the storm and which sections have evidence of condition or work.

blocks.text: For a new submission or renewal, confirm the building and get the roof’s installation and repair history. Ask for a dated inspection or contractor record tied to the roof sections when condition is material to the review. Keep the weather finding with the evidence used for that decision date. When a report or repair record arrives later, add it with its own date so the prior review remains reproducible.

title: Best commercial property data APIs for insurance underwriting
description: Compare commercial insurance prefill, hazard data, and property APIs. See how to verify building identity, roof work, and flood exposure before a quote.
coverAlt: Aerial view of Brooklyn Army Terminal, with the small footprint returned by the city’s Building A identifier marked in gold for review.
coverCaption: The gold outline is the footprint returned by the city building-ID lookup. Aerial imagery from NYS ITS, spring 2024. Tax lot from NYC MapPLUTO 26v2.
intro: Start with Cotality for building prefill and reconstruction cost. Evaluate Moody’s CAPE for imagery-derived roof and building attributes, Verisk for commercial underwriting reports, and Guidewire HazardHub for peril and fire-protection inputs. First Street provides modeled flood depth and damage. Ageospatial and Invariant Earth are options for teams that want to inspect the evidence behind property fields. Whatever you buy, test a submission where a single address covers multiple buildings.
takeaways: Match each line of the statement of values to a building before pulling construction or hazard attributes.
Keep permit issuance, the work it authorizes, and evidence of completion as separate fields.
Keep parcel-level hazard flags, a building’s modeled flood depth, and potential insured loss distinct in the record.

sections.heading: Which building is on the submission?

blocks.text: A statement of values lists the locations and values submitted for insurance. Consider a line for Building A at Brooklyn Army Terminal, 140 58th Street. The city’s municipal benchmarking report identifies Building A as Building Identification Number (BIN) 3257059 on tax lot 3057780001. The operator’s specification describes eight stories, a height of 89 feet, and approximately 500,000 square feet of floor area. We used those records to check what the building lookup returned.

The exact BIN matched a footprint in NYC’s building dataset on that tax lot. The footprint record reported a roof height of 14 feet and a construction year of 2022. Those values disagree with the operator’s description of Building A. Preserve the returned outline as a candidate, ask for a verified building plan or footprint, and leave building-level exposure pending. This is a useful test even for providers that report a confident address match.

The same campus illustrates what can happen downstream. Our parcel screen found a FEMA Zone AE overlap on 19.9% of the shoreline-clipped lot. Copying that result to a building record would change the scope of the evidence. After resolving the building outline, intersect it with the relevant map edition and keep the map, geometry and date used for the result.

sections.heading: What does a roof permit tell you about roof age?

blocks.text: NYC issued permit B01209484-I1-GC on June 17, 2026, for work including re-roofing on Building A. The description covers the main roof and tank house roofs and excludes the stair tower and mechanical penthouse roofs. Another record for October 6 covers temporary roof protection. Keep both events with their own dates and scopes.

The June record supports the scope of authorized work. To use it for roof age, look for a completion record, a signed contractor document, or inspection evidence that ties the installation date to the sections being insured. The checked records leave the last replacement date open. On renewal, keep the June and October evidence and append any new completion record with its own date.

sections.heading: What can an API prefill for commercial property?

blocks.text: Commercial property underwriters organize building information around construction, occupancy, protection, and exposure, often called COPE. Start with the submission and compare its answers with the records you can trace to that building. Keep the construction and hazard evidence alongside the values the insured has submitted for the property and its contents.

rows: Construction
Year built, stories, gross floor area, roof cover, and dates of recorded work.
Confirm which structure the source describes. Separate footprint area from total floor area and a permit date from completion.
Occupancy
Use documented for the premises, tenant entries, and building or suite identifiers.
Ask the applicant about actual operations, storage, and vacancies. A property’s land-use category describes a different unit than a tenant’s operation.
Protection
Documented fire protection, hydrant and station context, and system inspection records.
Verify sprinkler coverage and condition for the premises being insured. Use the carrier’s data rules for protection class.
Exposure
Map or modeled evidence for flood, wildfire, wind, and surrounding properties.
Save whether the analysis used an address pin, parcel or footprint. Keep the map edition or scenario, and separate hazard intensity from damage.
Reported values
Building, business personal property, and business interruption values in the submission, plus a reconstruction estimate where available.
Reconcile valuation scope with the insured. Check the estimator’s assumptions about materials, local costs, and excluded items.

sections.heading: Which providers should you test?

blocks.text: The options below are based on public product documentation. Invariant publishes this guide and makes Invariant Earth. The Brooklyn example tests public records directly and gives you an input to run through a trial or demo with each provider.

rows: Cotality
Commercial prefill, occupancy information, and commercial reconstruction cost estimates.
A multi-building site with a cost result tied to each building and a list of assumptions behind the estimate.
Moody’s CAPE
Commercial building and roof attributes from imagery, including condition ratings, reason codes, and change detection.
The imagery date and building ID for each condition result. Ask how the API and review interface handle unclear imagery or more than one roof on a schedule line.

Commercial underwriting reports through its API, including U.S. LOCATION and ProMetrix products.
Which U.S. report covers your commercial portfolio, the property ID it uses, and the fields returned at building versus location level.

An API for property characteristics, peril scores, and fire-suppression context.
The underlying variables, source dates, and the location geometry used for a flood or fire-protection result.
ZestyAI
Roof age and condition signals from imagery and records, with an API for its roof age estimates.
Whether the result is an estimate or based on observed work, which roof sections it covers, and whether the product supports your property types.
First Street
Modeled flood depths and damage metrics with scenario, return period, and time horizon.
A footprint result and a coordinate-only case. Verify how the model reports depth when an outline is unavailable.
Ageospatial
Building evidence for insurers drawn from imagery, maps, records, and documents.
How a line on a schedule is tied to a footprint, how conflicting building attributes surface, and what history can be exported.
ATTOM
Property characteristics such as year built, construction type, and roof cover in its property API.
A large commercial property split across structures. Ask which fields describe the primary structure and which aggregate across the site.
West Kite
Commercial property records and permits tied to properties, with dated sources.
A permit lookup for Building A and a walkthrough of how the API preserves the filing date, issuance, scope, and later status.

Location and parcel context, including hazard layers and field-level provenance and status.

sections.heading: Run the trial on your own book

blocks.text: Build a small reference set with a single-building property, a campus where buildings share an address, a partial roof replacement, and an unmatched location. title: Historical parcel boundaries API guide for splits and mergers
description: Trace an old parcel ID through a split or merger. Compare two real NYC tax map changes with dated boundaries, source queries, and a downloadable crosswalk.
coverAlt: Side-by-side boundary maps show Brooklyn block 3947 before and after its November 20 split. Lot 1 shrinks from about 45,290 to 24,121 square feet, and new lot 105 takes about 21,169 square feet.
coverCaption: Brooklyn block 3947. Same scale before and after. Boundaries from MapPLUTO 26v2 and NYC Tax Lot Polygon, checked against tax map alteration 738545. Areas are calculated from mapped geometry.
intro: A historical parcel lookup needs two things. The boundary that applied on the date you care about, and the relation between that parcel and the lots that came before or after it. A current parcel ID can survive even when its footprint changes. In Brooklyn on November 20, 2026, lot 1 on block 3947 kept its ID after a split, with about 53% of its former mapped area. A merger on another block that day retired two IDs and enlarged a third.
takeaways: Store dated geometry separately from the parcel number and keep both versions when the source preserves the same ID.
Use the local alteration record to tell a split from a merger, a map correction, or a new survey.
Validate the match with the old and new geometries, then keep source edition, change date, and observation date in the result.

sections.heading: A split where the old ID stayed in use

blocks.text: On Brooklyn block 3947, NYC’s older tax map shows one lot, numbered 1, at the Atlantic Avenue end of the block. The November 20 map shows lot 1 and lot 105 separated by a new internal boundary. Alteration 738545 labels lot 1 affected and lot 105 new. The borough, block, and lot identifier, known as a BBL in New York City, gives lot 1 the same value of 3039470001 on both versions.

The predecessor footprint measured about 45,290 square feet in the earlier geometry. After the split, the two footprints measured about 24,121 and 21,169 square feet. A query for the old BBL against today’s parcel layer can return lot 1 successfully and still omit almost half of the original footprint. The crosswalk returns both successors for an old record and assigns each boundary its own record ID.

sections.heading: A merger where two IDs disappeared

blocks.text: On Brooklyn block 3373, alteration 739346 marks lots 1 and 2 as dropped and lot 57 as affected. The prior map shows all three at the Broadway end of the block. The later map shows one enlarged lot 57. A lookup for either dropped BBL in the later geometry returned no row, but both historical footprints intersect the enlarged successor. The crosswalk also carries the old version of lot 57 forward to its expanded version.

intro: A commercial real estate lender can use property data APIs to identify collateral, find recorded instruments, and flag items for title, valuation, or flood review. Property and infrastructure diligence marketed for credit teams.

title: How to screen a truck depot with a 5 MW service limit
description: Use truck schedules, parcel access, and utility evidence to screen an EV fleet charging site. A 99-truck example shows when a 5 MW limit can work.
coverAlt: Modeled demand at a truck depot over 24 hours. Charging on arrival peaks at 5.13 MW around 6 p.m. Spreading the same charging energy over parked hours peaks at 1.45 MW.
coverCaption: Illustrative 15-minute demand at the meter using NREL warehouse-delivery operating patterns. Both schedules deliver the same charging energy and include 400 kW of other site demand.
intro: A 5 MW service limit can work for a truck charging depot when enough trucks stay parked long enough. Start with the energy each truck needs before its next dispatch, the time it can stay plugged in, and the load the rest of the site already uses. In our 99-truck example, charging on arrival peaks at 5.13 MW at the meter. Spreading the same energy over parked hours reduces the peak to 1.45 MW. The same 5 MW limit falls short when all trucks have only three hours.
takeaways: Model the busy dispatch day with return times, departure deadlines, required battery energy, and realistic charger limits.
Route a loaded truck to the proposed gate and draw its movement inside the yard. A parcel close to the interstate can still have an unusable entrance.
Ask the serving utility for the meter limit, service date, upgrade scope, and rate for each phase. Compare those terms with the site and truck commitments.

sections.heading: What changes when trucks charge overnight?

blocks.text: We built an example day from 99 single-shift operating patterns published with Brennan Borlaug and colleagues’ 2021 study. Each pattern represents one truck in the example, with its published route mileage and return and departure times. The model repeats that day, rounds each parking window inward to complete 15-minute intervals, and assumes 1.8 kWh per mile at the battery and 92% charging efficiency. Each truck can draw up to 100 kW AC at its port. Other site demand stays at 400 kW. This is a constructed fleet day using published inputs.

blocks.text: The two overnight schedules each assume one working port per truck, constant efficiency, and no battery storage. Vehicle charging power can fall as batteries fill. Late returns, reserve requirements, charger downtime, and shared cabinets can change what is possible. Test those cases with your actual trucks before treating the lower peak as a design input.

sections.heading: Screen a depot parcel near I-35

blocks.text: Pick the interchange your trucks will actually use. In Texas, local truck routes and posted restrictions can change the last mile. Check the route in both directions with the dimensions and loaded weight of your tractor and trailer. Review the driveway and traffic movements with the road authority or local jurisdiction before you rely on a route.

rows: Truck access
Route to the actual gate, turn restrictions, clearances, posted bridge limits, approach grade, and space to queue without blocking the road.
Usable yard
Parcel and survey, swept paths for a loaded truck, parking and trailer movements, charger cable reach, and areas needed for maintenance and emergency access.
Land and approvals
Documented site control, zoning and use permissions, drainage and flood screening, access and construction rights, and the easements required for service.
Utility service
Named utility and delivery point, current interval demand, proposed incremental and total import by phase, energization milestones, dependencies, and project cost responsibility.
Backup charging
An accessible station with a compatible connector and enough room for the fleet’s vehicles. Confirm access, operating hours, current port availability, and fallback terms with the operator.

blocks.text: Advance a parcel when the truck path, concept layout, and service path can all support the same dispatch plan. A parcel whose only workable gate sends tractor-trailers across a weight-restricted bridge stays off the shortlist until there is a documented alternate route. A parcel with good access and a utility date after the planned truck delivery needs a phased fleet plan or a different site.

sections.heading: Which data and APIs answer which questions?

rows: How much energy is needed before dispatch?
Fleet telematics, dispatch logs, and vehicle specifications. The national lab’s EVI-X tools support fleet and charging analysis.
Use arrival time, next departure, state of charge and usable battery capacity. Check charger-to-vehicle compatibility and how power changes during a session.
Can the truck reach the parcel?
A truck-routing API such as ArcGIS, together with state and local route restrictions.
Set the right truck dimensions and route to the actual gate. Confirm posted and private restrictions, then review the turns on the site plan.
Is a backup charger usable?
DOE’s Alternative Fueling Station Locator tracks station status, access, connectors, and maximum vehicle class where available.
Check the date and confirm with the operator. A listed vehicle class describes physical access. It cannot establish the current wait time, reserved capacity, or access rights.
What can I learn about the parcel and nearby infrastructure?
Invariant Earth’s catalog lists parcel, terrain, floodplain, and nearby grid-asset fields.
Retain the source, vintage and field status. Use them to eliminate or prioritize parcels and take the proposed load to the serving utility.

sections.heading: What to send the utility before you sign a lease

blocks.text: Send the parcel and proposed service location, fleet and port counts by phase, the requested service dates, and a busy-day load profile showing both charging and other site demand. Identify the charge-management limit you can enforce and explain how the fleet will operate when a charger is down or a shift gets back late. Ask which study and agreements are required, which upgrades or easements are on the critical path, and what deposits or construction costs the customer would carry.

Ask for the applicable tariff and the meter’s billing rules, including demand charges and time-of-use periods. A lower modeled peak helps evaluate the design. Your business case also depends on energy delivered, the rate and any contractual obligations. For a candidate with an existing service, confirm which load and delivery date the utility can support for your phase and configuration.

dataset.description: Four public PJM study records for two linked solar requests at Nottingham 138 kV in Harrison County, Ohio. The comparison includes dated MW fields, project-level cost estimates, changes between study phases, and source URLs and fingerprints.
